newsitem.title: FRANCE: French manufacturing sector weak in November.
newsitem.headline: French manufacturing sector weak in November.

text.p: French manufacturing production fell in November last year for the third consecutive month, confirming the weak state of the economy.

Figures released by national statistics institute INSEE on Wednesday showed however that a broader measure of industrial output rose for the first time since July thanks to a 3.1 percent jump in production at food companies.
Economists said the main issue now was whether the sharp rise in the dollar against the franc would boost exports and production, and whether that would be enough to create jobs.
Industrial production excluding energy, agri-food businesses and construction -- considered the best measure of manufacturing output -- fell 0.3 percent in November.
The decline, which came after a sharp 1.1 percent drop in October, meant production was up 1.1 percent in the three months to November compared with the same period last year.
Industrial production, excluding construction, rose 0.2 percent in November from the previous month and was up 1.7 percent in the three months to November compared to 1995.

"It was soft, which is not a big surprise. It's clear the economy had no momentum at the end of last year," Sean Shepley, CS First Boston international economist said. "But since then we've had a marked weakening of the exchange rate which is going to help stimulate growth."

The franc fell as low as 5.5453 against the U.S. dollar on Wednesday, the lowest it's been since June 16, 1994. So far this year the franc has tumbled 6.9 percent and is 13.6 percent weaker than its lowest level last year.

Patrick Mange, economist at Deutsche Bank, said the weakening of the currency against the Italian lira, peseta and sterling would also help French production but that it was very difficult to quantify how significant the impact would be.

"The transmission mechanism is very difficult to assess. I would say as time lapses more and more without investment, the chance companies will start to invest becomes higher as they haven't invested enough for three or four years," he said.
However he said, "what we have seen in past business surveys, is that foreign orders are tending to increase and domestic demand remains relatively sluggish."
With the French economic growth still feeble and the unemployment rate at a record 12.7 percent, the government faces a stiff task creating new jobs, economists said.

Mange also said that with capacity utilisation relatively low in France, a boost to demand from overseas would more likely lead to investment in modernisation and rationalisation which would not necessarily be positive for jobs in the short term.

Economists said one favourable aspect of the production report was that there were several revisions to past figures. Eric Chaney put the cumulated upward revision to industrial production at 0.4 percentage point.
Looking ahead he said output in December would have been hit by a nation-wide truck drivers strike, but cold weather may have boosted energy production.
